prompt: A service raises its time-based availability target from 99.9% to 99.99% over the same monthly window. What changes operationally?

options.text: The allowed downtime grows because the percentage is larger
options.explanation: Incorrect. A higher successful-time target leaves less time for unavailability.

options.text: The downtime allowance becomes ten times smaller, making detection and recovery speed more important
options.explanation: Correct. The unavailable share falls from one part in a thousand to one part in ten thousand.

options.text: No operational change is needed if the target is only documentation
options.explanation: Incorrect. A target should drive measured behaviour and recovery planning; relabelling does not improve the service.

options.text: The target proves stored data can never be lost
options.explanation: Incorrect. Availability concerns successful service; data-loss risk is durability.

workedExample: Keep the measurement window fixed and compare the remaining failure allowance. An extra nine removes most of the old downtime budget, so a manual response that fit the previous target may consume the new one. Check detection, failover and recovery against that smaller allowance.

prompt: An object store advertises 99.999999999% durability and a hypothetical time-based 99.9% monthly availability commitment. A product manager asks: "So we'll basically never be unable to read a file?" What's the accurate answer?

options.text: Yes; eleven nines means effectively always readable
options.explanation: Incorrect. Durability is about data not being *lost*; it says nothing about whether you can reach the data at a given moment.

options.text: Yes, as long as you enable versioning
options.explanation: Incorrect. Versioning protects against accidental overwrites and deletes, not against the service being unreachable.

options.text: No; eleven nines durability means about 1 in 10¹¹ reads will fail
options.explanation: Incorrect. Durability is measured per object per year (probability of loss), not per read. Failed reads are an availability matter.

options.text: No; durability describes loss risk, while this time-based availability target allows roughly 43 minutes of unavailability in a 30-day month
options.explanation: Correct. The object can be safely stored on many disks yet temporarily unreachable due to network, control-plane or regional problems. The 99.9% SLA is the relevant number for 'can I read it right now?'

workedExample: Ask two separate questions: will the object still exist, and can the service return it now? Durability concerns the first; availability concerns the second. A safely stored object can remain unreachable during a network or service outage. The hypothetical 99.9% time-based monthly commitment allows some unavailable time; its measurement and exclusions determine what counts. If access is critical, evaluate caching, delivery paths and regional failure recovery rather than relying on the durability figure.

prompt: Two incidents last equally long. One fails a small share of requests overnight; the other fails most requests at peak traffic. Under a request-based SLO, how should their error-budget impact be compared?

options.text: Count degraded minutes only; their impact is equal
options.explanation: Incorrect. That ignores both traffic volume and the share of requests that failed.

options.text: Count failed requests relative to the allowance for the SLO window
options.explanation: Correct. A request-based budget weights the failures actually experienced by requests, so the peak incident can consume much more.

options.text: Use only the largest failure percentage reached during either incident
options.explanation: Incorrect. Duration and request volume also determine how many requests failed.

options.text: Ignore partial failures unless every request fails
options.explanation: Incorrect. Partial outages still produce bad requests that consume the budget.

workedExample: Identify the SLI's unit before measuring impact. A request-based availability SLI counts good and bad requests across the chosen window. The same number of incident minutes can contain very different numbers of bad requests. Use the actual counts and apply the agreed budget policy.

prompt: Which statements about SLIs, SLOs, SLAs and error budgets are **true**? Select all that apply.

options.text: An SLA is normally set looser than the internal SLO for the same service
options.explanation: Correct. The gap means you breach your own objective, and react, before you owe customers credits.

options.text: When the error budget is exhausted, a common policy is to pause risky releases and focus on reliability
options.explanation: Correct. This is the core of an error-budget policy: the budget turns the speed-versus-stability argument into an agreed rule.

options.text: A 100% availability SLO is the ideal target for any user-facing service
options.explanation: Incorrect. 100% is unachievable, users can't tell the difference beyond their own network's reliability, and it leaves no budget for change. Google SRE explicitly argues against it.

options.text: The SLI is the contractual penalty paid when targets are missed
options.explanation: Incorrect. The SLI is the measurement itself (e.g. share of requests succeeding under 300 ms). Penalties belong to the SLA.

options.text: With request-based availability, an outage at peak hour consumes more budget than the same-length outage overnight
options.explanation: Correct. More requests fail at peak, so more of the budget is spent, which matches the real user impact.

workedExample: An SLI measures service behaviour, an SLO sets the desired level, and an SLA records a contractual commitment and consequences. The error budget is the allowed share of bad service outside the SLO. A request-based budget is consumed by failed requests, so an otherwise identical peak-hour outage spends more than an overnight one. Teams can agree to pause risky changes when the budget is exhausted; that is a policy based on user impact.
